newsitem.title: ISRAEL: INTERVIEW-Elscint sees future in strategic alliances.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Elscint sees future in strategic alliances.

text.p: Facing an uphill battle for market share in a slow-growth market for medical-imaging equipment, Israel's Elscint Ltd is forming alliances with competitors, president Jonathan Adereth said on Tuesday.
"Elscint is positioning itself in the centre of the circle with the giant companies at the perimeter," Adereth told Reuters.

This week the company, a unit of Elbit Medical Imaging, signed an agreement with GE Medical Systems, a subsidiary of the U.S. General Electric Co, forming a joint venture company to develop and produce nuclear medical-imaging equipment.

The agreement follows a pact signed in December with Germany's Siemens AG to develop and manufacture assemblies for computerised tomography. Last September, Elscint sealed a deal with the medical systems division of Philips Electronics NV to market its VariCam nuclear medical-imaging system in Japan.

The three companies are among Elscint's biggest competitors in the medical-imaging market. Elscint also has agreements with Silicon Graphics and Agfa, and Adereth said he expects more such agreements to follow.
"Everyone in the industry said there will be a consolidation....and we thought, if there's going to be a consolidation, we don't want to be one of the companies that will leave," explained Adereth.
He said he expected other medical-imaging makers to follow the same strategy.

The global market for medical-imaging devices, which use a range of technologies like ultrasound for diagnosis, has been hit by cost-cutting drives by health authorities and the maturing of the market, said analysts.
Adereth estimated Elscint, with sales in the first nine months of 1996 of $226 million, had only a seven percent share of the global medical-imaging market and saw little prospect of a break-out.

"It is known that Elscint in terms of technology is equal or better than the others," he said. "But for years we haven't been able to break 10 percent market shares, even in our leading line of nuclear medicine."

He estimated that together Elscint and GE controlled about a fifth of the $600 million nuclear medicine market, but that the joint venture could expand their share by reducing development and manufacturing costs and improving time-to-market.
"The target is to double the market share of the two companies," Adereth said.

"I think it's a very good move. Here are two companies who have modest market share in nuclear medicine," said Lehman Brothers analyst Theodor Kundtz, who covers the company. "They could have a stronger position in the market...as a much stronger No. 2 player."

Kundtz, who slashed his 1997 earnings outlook for Elscint last November to $0.40 a share from an earlier estimate of $1.05, said it was too early to tell what the impact of the alliances would be. He said he was holding to his forecast for the time being.
